newsitem.title: USA: Internet groups hail court, opponents seek new law.
newsitem.headline: Internet groups hail court, opponents seek new law.

text.p: An appreciative Internet community reacted with jubilation Thursday when the Supreme Court recognised the unique characteristics of cyberspace and struck down a law restricting indecent speech online.

But supporters of the law warned the court's action overturning the 1996 Communications Decency Act left children exposed to inappropriate, pornographic material that is widely available on the Internet. They pledged to pressure Congress to enact a more narrowly tailored law.

The law was never in effect as lower courts set it aside until legal challenges were resolved. But many Internet users feared the broadly worded restrictions would have chilled free expression across the global computer network.
The court agreed, ruling 7-2 that all key parts of the law violated the First Amendment by impinging on otherwise permissible speech among adults.

"Today's opinion defines the First Amendment for the next century," said David Sobel, legal counsel for the Electronic Privacy Information Centre, one of dozens of groups that asked the court to strike down the law.

In cyberspace, those on the Internet learned almost immediately of the decision when the Citizens Internet Empowerment Coalition, representing many of the plaintiffs, changed a graphic image on more than 12,000 Internet sites.
The animated picture, which for weeks had asked "Will online free speech survive," was changed to "Victory in the Supreme Court -- online free speech will survive."

Users also posted messages praising the ruling at various sites. On Wired magazine's "Hotwired" site, a long-running debate and discussion on the law first heard about the decision from a user named Samuel.
"I'm having two beers tonight," Samuel wrote. "One to toast the unanimous decision and one to toast the lot of you argumentative, stubborn, wonderful bastards."
The citizens coalition broadcast a press conference in Washington D.C. live over its Web site (http://www.ciec.org) and posted the full text of the Supreme Court ruling.

Internet companies, worried that the law would slow the booming growth of the Internet, also praised the ruling and said parents could use existing technology to prevent children from accessing pornographic material.

"It's an important victory for anyone who cares about free speech or the future of the Internet," Microsoft Corp. chairman Bill Gates said. "Today, there are other means of controlling material that parents find objectionable."

Supporters of the law countered that children were at risk without the legal protection. Sen. Dan Coats, an Indiana Republican who was one of the authors of the law, charged that "a judicial elite is undermining democratic attempts to address pressing social problems."
"The court did not necessarily rule out more specific regulatory methods," added Sen. Christopher Bond, a Missouri Republican.
Cathy Cleaver, director of legal policy at the Family Research Council in Washington, said the court's opinion left room for Congress to write a narrower law to protect children.

"As of today, the floodgates are open and pornographers can invite children in," Cleaver said. "But we're not going to stop fighting for protection for kids on-line. We will go back (to Congress) and you will be seeing a more narrowly drafted statute."
In its decision, the court noted that prior laws banning transmission of "obscene" materials and child pornography over any medium remain in force and would apply to the Internet.

President Clinton, whose administration argued in favour of the CDA at the Supreme Court, said he continued to back provisions of the law against obscenity. But he said he would meet with industry leaders, teachers, parents and librarians soon to develop techological solutions to protect children.
"With the right technology and rating systems, we can help ensure that our children don't end up in the red light district of cyberspace," Clinton said.
